title: Pull Push Legs 6 days Program Review
summary: He reviews viewer Muskox's 6-day PPL: barbell compounds in the morning, machine and dumbbell work at a workplace gym, and martial arts (boxing, Muay Thai, BJJ) five afternoons a week. He broadly approves but suggests evolving set schemes, lower top-end reps (10-15 rather than up to 20), supersets of non-competing movements, a band-fly giant set on push 2, controlled leg-raise reps, and nucleus overload for the lagging arms.

claims.claim: Reviewing beginner and intermediate programmes leaves little to say; programmes for people with special constraints are more interesting.
Military press, bench, weighted pull-up and Pendlay row are pretty much all the compound movements you need for overall development, apart from a few muscle groups.
Training each body part twice a week suits most people.

A naturally gifted lower body is a big bodybuilding advantage: it's where you lift the most weight and need the most tonnage, so if it grows easily you save a lot of training time to spend elsewhere. He cites Jeff Nippard's rant on this.
Tonnage converts into time once intensity and volume are taken into account.

Doing the first lift of the day in low reps (strength) and the second in higher reps (variation) is smart; it's what he does too. You can also rotate which lift serves as the strength or variation movement across days.
Evolving rep range (start at the bottom of the range, add reps until all sets reach the top, then add weight) is in his opinion the best way to progress.
Martial artists, like bodybuilders, never stop learning; someone who trains several disciplines needs to manage recovery to perform.
Many people who are unhappy or depressed aren't doing enough; work is happiness, the way he was raised, and seeing work as slavery is counter-intuitive to him.

On weighted pull-ups he prefers high intensity and low reps; consider evolving sets as well as reps, e.g. 3-5 sets of 4-8, accepting a short-term tonnage dip for faster progression and shorter strength work.
Bent-over rows at 4x8-12 is a rep range he loves.

He advises replacing lat pulldowns with pull-ups, especially for martial artists, using variations such as fat grips, towel grips, slow negatives or explosive reps for athletic carryover; keep pulldowns if you like their different load and stretch.
On heavy curls you can cheat on every set: use a weight you can only do 7-8 clean reps with, then cheat extra reps. It raises intensity without much more injury risk.
Face pulls belong at the high end of the rep spectrum, around 20 reps.
When supersetting, raise intensity, e.g. 4x10-15 instead of 3x12-20, so tonnage stays similar but intensity rises and cardio demand increases.
5x5-8 is potentially the perfect rep range for the military press.
Try once swapping the order of paused bench and military press to see if performance or shoulder feeling changes.
Apart from face pulls and some curls, going up to 20 reps enters territory where strength returns to baseline between sets; 10-15 or even 8-12 is more conducive to progression.
Supersetting two triceps movements is fine as long as they don't tire the same head, e.g. pushdowns (no long head) with overhead extensions.
He recently found that doing skull crushers inside a giant set of presses makes his presses stronger, because he can activate the triceps long head during the press.
5x5-8 on back squat is high volume; try an evolving set scheme of 3-5 sets of 5-8.
Depending on leverages, hip thrusts are more glute-focused and RDLs more hamstring and lower-back focused.
On leg day always start with the back squat; unlike presses, he would never swap the order.
He doubts cable shrugs give much stretch; barbell shrugs are unmatched. The stretch is the most important hypertrophy factor for traps, and 20 reps is a good shrug range.
Superset leg curls with leg extensions; if your legs are already developed you can drop them and do upper-body work (rear delts, light pull-ups) even on leg day.
He dislikes AMRAP hanging leg raises because the last reps become swinging, cheated junk; do the first set, then aim for one rep fewer on each following set.
Pendlay rows are popular with his subscribers but not a movement everyone needs; 5x5-8 is a good range for rows.
For weighted chin-ups as a second movement, 6 sets of 6-10 gives similar tonnage to 4x8-12 but is more conducive to progression.

Try seated cable rows one arm at a time to really stretch the lat; if lats are a weak point, push progression but also add nucleus-overload-style extra pull-up volume, which punishes the lats without killing recovery.
Forced negatives are amazing for the biceps.
72 hours between arm sessions may suit some people, but if arms lag you might need 48-hour frequency.
5x5-8 is a perfect rep range for horizontal pressing.
Pairing close-grip bench (arms/chest) with Z-press (shoulders) at 4x8-12 gives freedom to manipulate volume and intensity.
Pec flies aren't worthless but aren't the best for shoulder health.

His challenge: replace machine pec flies with a giant set alternating resistance-band standing chest flies between each accessory (overhead extensions, lateral raises, rope pushdowns), for 4 rounds; bench day taxes cardio least, so a giant set complements it.
Legs are the easiest body part to train with only a barbell; his own leg training is 100% barbell movements.
5 sets of 3-5 on deadlift leaves room: if you get 5 on set 1 and 3 on the last you didn't push intensity; for more intensity do 4 sets or, as he does, 3 sets of 2-5.
Supersetting lower-body lifts is harder, so he wouldn't superset them except maybe power shrugs with ab work; he'd add a set to power shrugs (4x20).

Alternating posterior-chain and quad movements within a session matters: within-session frequency is as important as between-day frequency, because muscles recover within the session, allowing more tonnage.
For lagging arms, especially with long limbs, use nucleus overload for biceps and triceps; it pays off over time and can be done the same day.
Grapplers who grip constantly should train their finger extensors; martial artists should train the neck (e.g. neck bridges).
